label: copy phase (after the first output)
explanation: Broad copy-phase feature: fires on about 96% of copy-phase steps (t > L, i.e. recall_idx >= 1) and is essentially silent during the original phase and on the <DEL> step (about 0.1% of original-phase steps, which carry ~0% of the mass). Activation rate is flat across input token, L and n_digits. Magnitude depends on which token is being copied: out_tok b, j, e get about 2x the activation mass of c or i at the same firing rate. The top examples peak in the middle of the copy. It does not fire before the delimiter or on the delimiter step itself.

issues: The test scores reproduce exactly for phase == 2: P 0.956, R 0.999, F1 0.977, mass recall 1.000. All four activation quartiles have coverage of 0.996 or higher.
Missed activations: 2944 test steps, all in the original phase at t >= 3. Their activations are tiny (<=0.17 of max) and they hold 0.0% of the mass. This is scattered noise, not a pattern.

False positives (4.4% of copy steps) are partly organised by out_tok, which the explanation does not mention. Copy-phase firing rate is about 1.00 when out_tok is b, c, e, f, g, h, i, u, v, z, 0 or 3. It is lower for x (0.81), w (0.85), t (0.86), 2 (0.88), k (0.89), q (0.90) and y (0.90). The explanation's 'flat firing rate' claim covers only input token, L and n_digits, and those do check out. The b/j/e vs c/i magnitude claim also holds: mass share is 0.080 for b vs 0.031 for c, with both firing at about 100%. Dropping the low-rate tokens from the predicate would cost more recall than it gains in precision, so this does not support a better predicate.
Firing rate is flat by recall_idx (0.93 to 0.99) and by L (0.94 to 0.95). There is no position or length class of misses or false positives.
'Top examples peak in the middle of the copy' is a soft claim. The top examples do peak around recall_idx 3 to 5, but the peak looks tied to the output being b or j rather than to position. Minor.
